claim: Single-molecule magnetic tweezers have emerged as a powerful tool for studying membrane proteins, providing valuable insights into their biogenesis, interactions with drugs, and the effects of chaperones on their folding.
source: Single-molecule magnetic tweezers have emerged as a powerful tool for studying membrane proteins, providing valuable insights into their biogenesis, interactions with drugs, and the effects of chaperones on their folding (Hong et al., 2022; Petrosyan et al., 2021; Jefferson et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Hong et al., 2022; Petrosyan et al., 2021; Jefferson et al., 2018)

claim: Magnetic tweezers have extremely low spring constants that allow for constant low-force measurements.
source: Their extremely low spring constants allow for constant low-force measurements (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019

claim: The dig-antidig binding has a short lifetime of ~1 s at 25 pN and ~0.1 s at 50 pN.
source: Especially, the dig-antidig binding has a short lifetime of ~1 s at 25 pN and ~0.1 s at 50 pN (Van Patten et al., 2018), limiting the stable performance of experiments.
evidence: Supported by citation to Van Patten et al., 2018

claim: The tethering system using DBCO, traptavidin, and SpyTag has a lifetime of ~12 hr at 50 pN.
source: This tethering system has a lifetime of ~12 hr at 50 pN, a force level sufficient for most biomolecular interactions, covering up to 98% of surveyed protein folds.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract based on experimental measurements

claim: The new tethering system stability is over 100 times higher than the conventional dig/biotin system with a lifetime of only ~7 min at 45 pN.
source: The system stability is over 100 times higher than the conventional dig/biotin system with a lifetime of only ~7 min at 45 pN (Janissen et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison based on data from this study and cited reference (Janissen et al., 2014)

claim: The method allowed observation of structural transitions of a designer single-chained transmembrane homodimer for 9 hr at 12 pN.
source: By using this method, we were able to observe numerous structural transitions of a designer single-chained transmembrane homodimer for 9 hr at 12 pN and reveal its folding pathway including the hidden dynamics of helix-coil transitions.

claim: The Kramers rate framework yields a considerably low-speed limit of 21 ms for a helical hairpin formation in lipid bilayers.
source: The Kramers rate framework yields a considerably low-speed limit of 21 ms for a helical hairpin formation in lipid bilayers, compared to μs scale for soluble protein folding.
evidence: Result from applying Kramers rate theory to experimental data

claim: The folding speed limit for helical membrane proteins is considerably slower compared to μs scale for soluble protein folding.
source: The Kramers rate framework yields a considerably low-speed limit of 21 ms for a helical hairpin formation in lipid bilayers, compared to μs scale for soluble protein folding.
evidence: Comparison between measured data and established knowledge about soluble proteins

claim: The large discrepancy in folding speed is likely due to the highly viscous nature of lipid membranes, retarding the helix-helix interactions.
source: This large discrepancy is likely due to the highly viscous nature of lipid membranes, retarding the helix-helix interactions.

claim: Rapid noncovalent tethering approach using digoxigenin and biotin is commonly used to attach target molecules to solid supports.
source: Rapid noncovalent tethering approach using digoxigenin (dig) and biotin is commonly used to attach target molecules to solid supports (beads or chamber surface; Choi et al., 2022; Bauer et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2022; Moessmer et al., 2022; Pandey et al., 2022; Zhao and Woodside, 2021; Maciuba et al., 2021; Avellaneda et al., 2020; Gupta et al., 2020; Kostrz et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2018; Min et al., 2018; Hao et al., 2017; Yao et al., 2014; del Rio et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations showing common practice

claim: The bound complexes of dig-antidig dissociate at force ranges of tens of pN.
source: However, the bound complexes dissociate at force ranges of tens of pN (Van Patten et al., 2018; Janissen et al., 2014; Schlingman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Traptavidin is a streptavidin variant with ~17-fold slower biotin dissociation and ~eightfold stronger biotin binding.
source: The traptavidin is a streptavidin variant with ~17-fold slower biotin dissociation (off-rate constant ratio: koff,S/koff,T = 16.7) and ~eightfold stronger biotin binding (dissociation constant ratio: Kd,S/Kd,T = 8.3; Chivers et al., 2010), which can easily replace streptavidin variants typically used in single-molecule tweezers.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chivers et al., 2010

claim: Using 0.025–0.1 mM DBCO crosslinker was an optimal condition for bead surface modification.
source: We found that using 0.025–0.1 mM DBCO crosslinker was an optimal condition.

claim: Lower or higher DBCO concentrations (0.01 or 1 mM) resulted in unsuccessful conjugation to target molecules or nonspecific binding of beads to the surface.
source: Lower or higher concentrations, such as 0.01 or 1 mM, resulted in unsuccessful conjugation to target molecules or nonspecific binding of beads to the surface (Figure 3 and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental result shown in figure and data

claim: 0.05% (w/v) DDM detergent condition enabled the stable solubilization of membrane proteins along with the DBCO-mediated bead tethering.
source: Among various concentrations of diverse detergent/lipid molecules (Figure 3 and Figure 3—source data 1), we found that 0.05% (w/v) DDM detergent condition enabled the stable solubilization of membrane proteins along with the DBCO-mediated bead tethering (critical micelle concentration of DDM = ~0.01%).

claim: The method failed in tethering with short DNA handles, typically less than 500 bp.
source: We failed in the tethering with short handles, typically less than 500 bp as used in single-molecule tweezers (Choi et al., 2022; Moessmer et al., 2022; Kostrz et al., 2019; Min et al., 2018; Hao et al., 2017; Figure 3 and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental result with citations to typical handle lengths

claim: scTMHC2 was unfolded at 18.2±0.1 pN at a magnet speed of 0.5 mm/s.
source: We found that scTMHC2 was unfolded at 18.2±0.1 pN at a magnet speed of 0.5 mm/s (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which is consistent with a previous study (Lu et al., 2018).
evidence: Experimental measurement consistent with previous study

claim: For 98% of surveyed proteins, the most probable or average unfolding forces were measured to be less than 50 pN.
source: For 98% of them, the most probable or average unfolding forces were measured to be less than 50 pN, regardless of their molecular weights and used force-loading rates (Figure 4D and Figure 4—source data 1).

claim: The mean lifetime of the linkage system at 50 pN was estimated to be 11.7±1.5 hr.
source: We measured the survival probability of our linkage system over time at the upper-bound force and estimated the mean lifetime until bead detachment to be 11.7±1.5 hr (Figure 4E).

claim: The median lifetime of a conventional linkage system that uses 1 dig and 1 biotin is around 7 min at 45 pN.
source: In contrast, the median lifetime of a conventional linkage system that uses 1 dig and 1 biotin is very short, around 7 min at 45 pN (Janissen et al., 2014).

claim: The new system is at least 100 times more stable than the conventional system used in previous membrane protein studies.
source: This result demonstrates that our system is at least 100 times more stable than the conventional system used in the previous membrane protein studies.
evidence: Comparison of experimental data with cited reference

claim: The tweezer method can perform a large number of unfolding cycles with a single membrane protein, up to a thousand times on average.
source: Our tweezer method can also perform a large number of unfolding cycles with a single membrane protein, up to a thousand times on average (Figure 5A).

claim: The level of mean unfolding force and step size values remained almost constant over the thousand times pulling with a slope of ~10^-4 pN(nm)/cycle.
source: Nonetheless, the level of the mean values remained almost constant over the thousand times pulling (slope ~10–4 pN[nm]/cycle; Figure 5—figure supplement 2 for the DNA hairpin).

claim: The kinetic error can be approximated to be 3.7, 1.8, and 0.9% at 60, 200, and 1000 pulling cycles, respectively.
source: With correction of instrumental errors (Jacobson and Perkins, 2020; Cossio et al., 2015; Neupane and Woodside, 2016), the error of kinetics can be approximated to be 3.7, 1.8, and 0.9% at 60, 200, and 1000 pulling cycles, respectively.
evidence: Result from Monte Carlo simulations with instrumental error corrections

claim: All membrane proteins studied by single-molecule tweezers exhibit relatively large mechanical hysteresis with tens-of-pN gaps between their unfolding and refolding forces.
source: All membrane proteins studied by single-molecule tweezers exhibit relatively large mechanical hysteresis with tens-of-pN gaps between their unfolding and refolding forces, even at very low loading rates like 1 pN/s (Choi et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2022; Min et al., 2018; Min et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2018).

claim: The high stability of the tweezers allowed observation of persistent (un)folding transitions lasting for 9 hr at 12 pN.
source: The high stability of our tweezers allowed us to observe persistent (un)folding transitions lasting for a long time of 9 hr (Figure 6A).

claim: The extension distribution displayed four clear peaks, indicating that there are four major structural states.
source: The extension distribution displayed four clear peaks (Figure 6A, right), indicating that there are four major structural states.

claim: The Uc state is slightly more favorable than the Uh state (ΔGUc-Uh = –1.7 kBT) at 12 pN.
source: The Uc state is slightly more favorable than the Uh state (ΔGUc-Uh = –1.7 kBT), although this force is ~6 pN lower than the ~18 pN force level of the helix-to-coil transition during the stretching experiments (Figure 4C).

claim: The first unfolding transition (N-to-I1,2) is the rate-limiting step with the highest energy barrier (ΔG†N-to-I=7.8 kBT) and slowest rate (τN-to-I=381 s).
source: Even though the force application of 12 pN lowers the energy barrier for this transition, the barrier (rate) is still highest (slowest) among all transitions (ΔG†N-to-I=7.8 kBT and τN-to-I=381 s).

claim: Only the transitions between adjacent states are allowed such as N↔I1,2↔Uh↔Uc.
source: Moreover, only the transitions between adjacent states are allowed such as N↔I1,2↔Uh↔Uc (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claim: The helical domains of the Uh state would penetrate into the membrane by an average of ~1.0 nm at 12 pN.
source: While the random coil of the Uc state would be extracted out of the membrane as discussed in a previous section, the helical domains of the Uh state would penetrate into the membrane by an average of ~1.0 nm at 12 pN (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3; Methods).
evidence: Calculated from polymer models and experimental data

claim: The penetration depth of ~1.0 nm covers approximately one third of the bicelle membrane core of ~3.0 nm thickness.
source: This penetration covers approximately one third of the bicelle membrane core of ~3.0 nm thickness (Leite et al., 2022; Giudice et al., 2022; Murugova et al., 2022; Methods), similar to the so-called zigzag state defined in a previous study (Choi et al., 2019), where a similar penetration depth of ~1.0 nm was estimated at 8 pN for GlpG.
evidence: Comparison with cited membrane thickness values

claim: At 12 pN, a helical hairpin is marginally stable (ΔGI-Uh = –0.3 kBT).
source: At 12 pN, a helical hairpin is marginally stable (ΔGI-Uh = –0.3 kBT), whereas the finally folded state (the dimerized state of two helical hairpins) is ~10 times more stable (ΔGN-I = –3.2 kBT).

claim: The finally folded state (the dimerized state of two helical hairpins) is ~10 times more stable (ΔGN-I = –3.2 kBT) than a single helical hairpin.
source: At 12 pN, a helical hairpin is marginally stable (ΔGI-Uh = –0.3 kBT), whereas the finally folded state (the dimerized state of two helical hairpins) is ~10 times more stable (ΔGN-I = –3.2 kBT).

claim: The final dimerization is likely the primary stabilizing step for the native fold.
source: This indicates that the formation of the other helical hairpin alone does not significantly contribute to the native fold stability. Instead, the final dimerization is likely the primary stabilizing step.

claim: The estimated τω values are 184±0.06 ms for the coil-to-helix transition, 21.4±0.09 ms for the helical hairpin formation, and 48.7±0.11 ms for the final folding.
source: The estimated τω values for each structural transition are as follows: 184±0.06 ms for the coil-to-helix transition, 21.4±0.09 ms for the helical hairpin formation, and 48.7±0.11 ms for the final folding (helical hairpin formation plus dimerization).
evidence: Calculated from experimental data using Kramers equation

claim: The range of 21–184 ms for τω is considerably lower than the range of 1 μs – 1 ms for typical soluble proteins (>100 residues).
source: The range of 21–184 ms for τω is considerably lower than the range of 1 μs – 1 ms for typical soluble proteins (>100 residues; Gebhardt et al., 2010; Kubelka et al., 2004; Hagen et al., 1996; Schuler et al., 2002; Kubelka et al., 2006; Dumont et al., 2009; Chung and Eaton, 2013; Szczepaniak et al., 2019; see Kubelka et al., 2004 for other relevant literatures).

claim: The exceedingly low speed limits for the transitions could be due to the effect of very high viscosity of lipid membranes.
source: The exceedingly low speed limits for the transitions could be due to the effect of very high viscosity of lipid membranes.

claim: The viscosity of DMPC lipid membranes has been measured to be approximately 70–2.3×10^4 times higher than that of water.
source: Indeed, the viscosity of DMPC lipid membranes used in this study has been measured using various methods to be approximately 70–2.3×104 times higher than that of water (Nagao et al., 2017; Nojima and Iwata, 2014; Wu et al., 2013; Dimova et al., 2000; Bahri et al., 2005; Filippov et al., 2003; Figure 7—source data 1 for the measured viscosity values).

claim: Excluding the smallest and largest viscosity values, the range of the viscosity ratio between lipid membranes and water is approximately 1.1×10^2–3.9×10^3.
source: If we exclude the smallest and largest values to avoid potential artifacts, the range of the viscosity ratio between the lipid membranes and water is approximately 1.1×102–3.9×103.

claim: The maximum possible τω range in the absence of membrane viscosity is approximately 5.5 μs – 1.7 ms.
source: With this range of the viscosity ratios, we determined a maximum possible τω range of 5.5 μs – 1.7 ms in the absence of the membrane viscosity.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data and viscosity ratios

claim: The estimated τω range in the absence of membrane viscosity largely overlaps with the τω range for soluble proteins.
source: This rough estimate largely overlaps with the τω range for soluble proteins (Figure 7B), providing a tantalizing clue for the origin of the slow speed limits, i.e., the viscosity of lipid membranes.
evidence: Comparison of calculated values with literature values

claim: A helical hairpin is the minimal structural size for helical membrane proteins that require the tertiary folding.
source: A helical hairpin is the minimal structural size for helical membrane proteins that require the tertiary folding (Choi et al., 2019; Corin and Bowie, 2022; Krainer et al., 2018; Engelman and Steitz, 1981), although larger membrane proteins can fold via accrual of smaller structural units on the initial template (Choi et al., 2022; Corin and Bowie, 2022).

claim: A time scale of ~20 ms for the helical hairpin formation may be around the upper limit of folding speeds for the entire helical membrane proteome.
source: Thus, it is tempting to speculate that a time scale of ~20 ms for the helical hairpin formation may be around the upper limit of folding speeds for the entire helical membrane proteome.

claim: The coil-to-helix transition has a time scale of ~180 ms for τω, which is ~9 times slower than the helical hairpin formation.
source: The coil-to-helix transition has a time scale of ~180 ms for τω, which is ~9 times slower than the helical hairpin formation.

claim: A covalent DNA tethering with thiol-maleimide and amine-carboxyl linkages exhibited a minimum lifetime of ~23 hr at 45 pN.
source: A covalent DNA tethering with thiol-maleimide and amine-carboxyl linkages exhibited a minimum lifetime of ~23 hr at 45 pN (Janissen et al., 2014).

claim: Another DNA tethering method using multiple biotins and DBCOs showed a high stability with a mean lifetime of ~60 hr at 45 pN.
source: Another DNA tethering method using multiple biotins and DBCOs also showed a high stability with a mean lifetime of ~60 hr at 45 pN (Lin et al., 2023).

claim: The mean lifetime of the slowest kinetics for biotin-streptavidin tethering was measured as ~19 hr at 45 pN.
source: Although the anchoring geometry of the biotin-streptavidin tethering affected the lifetime distributions (Löf et al., 2019; Gruber et al., 2020), the mean lifetime of the slowest kinetics was measured as ~19 hr at 45 pN (Löf et al., 2019).

claim: The previous characterization of folding energy landscapes of helical membrane proteins was largely overestimated by 3–12 kBT due to the simple use of the kω ranges for soluble proteins.
source: This implies that the previous characterization of folding energy landscapes of helical membrane proteins (Choi et al., 2019; Min et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2018) was largely overestimated by 3–12 kBT due to the simple use of the kω ranges for soluble proteins (Figure 7B).
evidence: Inference from comparing new results with previous studies

claim: The range of kω values estimated for a helical membrane protein corresponds to 5.4 s^-1 to 46.7 s^-1, sharply contrasting to the range of 10^3–10^6 s^-1 for soluble proteins.
source: The range of τω values estimated for a helical membrane protein corresponds to very low level of the frequency factor, kω, ranging from 5.4 s–1 to 46.7 s–1, sharply contrasting to the range of 103–106 s–1 for soluble proteins.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data and comparison with literature

claim: The high membrane viscosity may be the microscopic origin for the prevalent mechanical hysteresis observed in membrane proteins.
source: The high membrane viscosity may also be the microscopic origin for the prevalent mechanical hysteresis observed in membrane proteins – to drive the tardy transitions, you should apply higher forces for unfolding and lower forces for refolding.
evidence: Speculative explanation connecting viscosity to observed hysteresis

claim: Changing solvent viscosity can alter folding pathways in soluble proteins according to simulation studies.
source: Simulation studies with soluble proteins have shown that changing solvent viscosity can alter folding pathways (Klimov and Thirumalai, 1997; Rhee and Pande, 2008), which may also be the case for membrane protein folding.
evidence: Cited from simulation studies and speculative extension to membrane proteins

claim: The robust magnetic tweezer approach is ~100 times more stable than the conventional method used for membrane protein studies.
source: In this study, we established a robust magnetic tweezer approach that is ~100 times more stable than the conventional method used for membrane protein studies.

claim: The folding speed limit for helical membrane proteins is exceedingly low compared to soluble proteins.
source: Our results revealed that the folding speed limit is exceedingly low compared to soluble proteins.

claim: scTMHC2 is a designed single-chain TM homodimer that consists of two identical monomers with two helices connected by a short peptide linker.
source: It should be pointed out that scTMHC2 was designed as a single-chained homodimer, which consists of two identical monomers with two helices connected by a short peptide linker (Lu et al., 2018; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A for its amino acid sequence).
evidence: Cited from previous study and shown in figure

claim: The TM helical part bounded by the RK and YW rings is ~3.0 nm, which matches the ~3.0 nm thickness of the bicelle membrane core.
source: Once finally folded, the ~3.0 nm TM helical part bounded by the RK and YW rings well matches the ~3.0 nm thickness of the bicelle membrane core (Leite et al., 2022; Giudice et al., 2022; Murugova et al., 2022; Figure 6C and Methods).
evidence: Comparison of calculated protein dimension with cited membrane thickness

claim: The pre-exponential factor (τω) provides an estimate of the fastest possible folding time for a protein.
source: In the Kramers rate theory (τfolding = τω∙exp[ΔG†/kBT]; Hänggi et al., 1990), the pre-exponential factor (τω) provides an estimate of the fastest possible folding time for a protein (Kubelka et al., 2004; Chung and Eaton, 2018).
evidence: Established theoretical framework from cited references

claim: The time scale of τω is considered as the so-called 'speed limit' of protein folding.
source: Thus, the time scale of τω is considered as the so-called 'speed limit' of protein folding (Kubelka et al., 2004; Chung and Eaton, 2018).

claim: The formation of a helical hairpin resulted in a significantly reduced speed limit by a factor of ~10^4, compared to soluble proteins of similar size.
source: Among three distinct transitions, the formation of a helical hairpin resulted in a significantly reduced speed limit by a factor of ~104, compared to soluble proteins of similar size (Kubelka et al., 2004).
evidence: Comparison of experimental result with cited reference

claim: The SpyTag/SpyCatcher conjugation was employed for DNA handle attachment to membrane proteins.
source: We employed the SpyTag/SpyCatcher conjugation for the DNA handle attachment (Min et al., 2016; Zakeri et al., 2012; Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Once SpyCatcher and SpyTag are bound, an isopeptide bond between the pair is spontaneously formed in 1–2 hr at 20–22°C.
source: Once the SpyCatcher and SpyTag are bound, an isopeptide bond between the pair is spontaneously formed in 1–2 hr at 20–22°C.

claim: The DBCO-azide conjugation does not require any catalytic enzymes or metal ions.
source: In this reaction, the azide-modified end of the construct was conjugated to the DBCO-coated bead without any catalytic enzymes or metal ions (Figure 2A).

claim: The DBCO conjugation process provides an advantage over other types of click reactions requiring transition metals or enzyme-catalyzed conjugation approaches.
source: This simple conjugation process provides an advantage over other types of click reactions requiring transition metals or enzyme-catalyzed conjugation approaches (Kim and Koo, 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Comparison with other methods cited in references

claim: The hydrophobic tails of detergents/lipids may decrease the overall conjugation efficiency by interfering with the hydrophobic DBCO moiety.
source: This is likely because the hydrophobic tails of detergents/lipids may decrease the overall conjugation efficiency by interfering with the hydrophobic DBCO moiety (Huynh et al., 2019).

claim: The best condition for DBCO-azide conjugation was in the absence of any detergents or lipids.
source: Indeed, the best condition was in the absence of any detergents or lipids (Figure 3; no detergents/lipids only during the conjugation step).

claim: Membrane proteins are sparsely tethered to the chamber surface, which kept them from aggregating even without detergents/lipids.
source: This situation is possible because membrane proteins are sparsely tethered to the chamber surface, which kept them from aggregating.

claim: The yield of the final construct with azide at one end and 2×biotin at the other end is ~10% of the SpyCatcher-DNA construct.
source: The yield of the final construct with azide at one end and 2×biotin at the other end is ~10% of the SpyCather-DNA construct.

claim: The critical micelle concentration of DDM is ~0.01%.
source: Among various concentrations of diverse detergent/lipid molecules (Figure 3 and Figure 3—source data 1), we found that 0.05% (w/v) DDM detergent condition enabled the stable solubilization of membrane proteins along with the DBCO-mediated bead tethering (critical micelle concentration of DDM = ~0.01%).

claim: The unfolding forces and step sizes of scTMHC2 appeared in the helix-coil transition zone bounded by two hypothetical unfolded states.
source: Its unfolding forces and step sizes appeared in the helix-coil transition zone bounded by two hypothetical unfolded states (Choi et al., 2019; Min et al., 2015 Figure 4C) – the unfolded polypeptide state with all helices fully unstructured (the unfolded coil state; Uc) and the unfolded helical state with all helices fully structured (Uh).
evidence: Experimental observation compared with polymer models

claim: The two unfolded states were modeled using the worm-like chain (WLC) and Kessler-Rabin (KR) polymer models for polypeptides and helices, respectively.
source: We modeled the two unfolded states using the worm-like chain (WLC) and Kessler-Rabin (KR) polymer models for polypeptides and helices, respectively (see Methods).

claim: At high forces, the TM helical portions of the Uh state are likely to be located at the water-membrane interface as they are highly stretched.
source: At high forces, the TM helical portions of the Uh state are likely to be located at the water-membrane interface as they are highly stretched.
evidence: Inference from force application and structural constraints

claim: At lower forces, TM helices can be inserted into the membrane with angles.
source: However, at lower forces, they can be inserted into the membrane with angles (Choi et al., 2019).

claim: Once the TM helices become unstructured (Uc state), the corresponding polypeptide portions are unlikely to be within the membrane due to an energetic cost of the polar backbone in contact with nonpolar lipid tails.
source: Once the TM helices become unstructured, as in the Uc state, the corresponding polypeptide portions are unlikely to be within the membrane due to an energetic cost of the polar backbone in contact with nonpolar lipid tails.

claim: Unfolding above the helix-coil transition zone will be a coupled event of unfolding and extraction from the membrane.
source: Thus, unfolding above the helix-coil transition zone will be a coupled event of unfolding and extraction from the membrane.

claim: It is unclear whether the membrane protein in the Uc state is entirely in water or at the water-membrane interface.
source: It is still unclear, however, whether the membrane protein in the Uc state is entirely in water or at the water-membrane interface.

claim: The fully unstructured protein may frequently bind and unbind from the bicelles in solution through the interactions with hydrophobic side chains.
source: The fully unstructured protein may frequently bind and unbind from the bicelles in solution through the interactions with hydrophobic side chains.

claim: 50 pN was set as an upper bound for the robustness test because 98% of surveyed proteins unfold below this force.
source: Since protein folding involves numerous noncovalent interactions, ranging from hundreds to thousands of inter-residue interactions (Gromiha and Selvaraj, 2004), most biomolecular interactions could be studied below the 50 pN. Thus, the 50 pN was set as an upper bound for our robustness test.
evidence: Reasoning based on survey data and cited reference

claim: Protein folding involves numerous noncovalent interactions, ranging from hundreds to thousands of inter-residue interactions.
source: Since protein folding involves numerous noncovalent interactions, ranging from hundreds to thousands of inter-residue interactions (Gromiha and Selvaraj, 2004), most biomolecular interactions could be studied below the 50 pN.

claim: The measured variables for individual molecules appear consistent over the thousand cycles within inherent stochastic nature of protein (un)folding.
source: The measured variables for individual molecules, such as the unfolding force and step size, appear consistent over the thousand cycles within inherent stochastic nature of protein (un)folding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: The values are affected by the force calibration error due to variations in bead size (~3% in diameter).
source: However, the values are affected by the force calibration error due to variations in bead size (~3% in diameter; Methods).

claim: The relative SD (RSD) for unfolding force and step size was estimated to be 7.0 and 10.4%.
source: The relative SD (RSD; defined as the ratio of the SD to the mean) was estimated to be 7.0 and 10.4% (Figure 5B, right), mainly reflecting the fluctuations from the stochastic barrier crossing.

claim: A systematic trend between the unfolding force/size and the progress of pulling cycles may indicate a temporal alteration of the protein fold, such as protein aging effect via oxidative damage.
source: A systematic trend between the unfolding force/size and the progress of pulling cycles may indicate a temporal alteration of the protein fold, such as protein aging effect via oxidative damage.

claim: Single-molecule tweezers have revealed the phenomenon of protein aging or folding fatigue of several soluble proteins.
source: Indeed, single-molecule tweezers have revealed the phenomenon of the protein aging or folding fatigue of several soluble proteins (Valle-Orero et al., 2017; Kellermayer et al., 2001).

claim: The method offers the ability to quantify the oxidative damage on membrane protein folds and investigate how chaperone proteins or ligands interact with the changing folds over time.
source: Thus, our method offers the ability to quantify the oxidative damage on membrane protein folds and investigate how chaperone proteins or ligands interact with the changing folds over time.

claim: The kinetic error trend was decomposed into fast and slow decays, with τ=52 and 1223 cycles, respectively.
source: The kinetic error trend was decomposed into the fast and slow decays, with τ=52 and 1223 cycles, respectively (Figure 5D and Methods).

claim: Recent studies have managed to capture transitions for short time scales of tens-to-hundreds of seconds at 5–7 pN.
source: Recent studies have managed to capture the transitions for short time scales of tens-to-hundreds of seconds at 5–7 pN (Choi et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2022).

claim: At 5-7 pN, once the proteins have folded, it is unlikely to unfold again within the practical time scales of experiments.
source: However, the force level is much more favorable to the native states. As a result, once the proteins have folded, it is unlikely to unfold again within the practical time scales of experiments.

claim: The force of 12 pN is close to the mean force of the most probable unfolding and refolding forces (~13 pN) for scTMHC2.
source: In light of this, upon complete unfolding of scTMHC2 to the Uc state above the helix-coil transition zone, we decreased the force to 12 pN, which is close to the mean force of the most probable unfolding and refolding forces (~13 pN; Lu et al., 2018).
evidence: Experimental design based on cited reference

claim: The nonlinear constrained iterative deconvolution method is independent of kinetic models.
source: To reconstruct the folding energy landscape (ΔG[l]) at 12 pN, we employed a nonlinear constrained iterative deconvolution method (Gebhardt et al., 2010; Woodside et al., 2006), which is independent of the kinetic models (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 for its test with simulated data; see Methods).

claim: The deconvolution approach eliminates the fluctuation noise of the bead and handles by iteratively deconvoluting the initial probability density of the measured extension.
source: This approach eliminates the fluctuation noise of the bead and handles by iteratively deconvoluting the initial probability density of the measured extension (P[l]).

claim: The observed (un)folding times were corrected for the limited temporal resolution and tethered bead-handle effect.
source: The observed times were corrected for the limited temporal resolution and tethered bead-handle effect (Jacobson and Perkins, 2020; Cossio et al., 2015; τ(un)folding; see Methods).
evidence: Description of data correction procedure with citations

claim: Rapid interconversions between the Uh and Uc states (helix-coil transitions) were observed at constant 12 pN.
source: At the constant 12 pN, we observed rapid interconversions between the Uh and Uc states, i.e., the helix-coil transitions (see the zoomed-in traces in Figure 6A).

claim: The hysteresis effect arises likely because the first unfolding transition (N-to-I1,2) is the rate-limiting step.
source: This hysteresis effect arises likely because the first unfolding transition (N-to-I1,2) is the rate-limiting step.

claim: The helix-coil transitions likely accompany the insertion and extraction of TM helices in and out of the bicelle membrane.
source: This estimation suggests that the helix-coil transitions likely accompany the insertion and extraction of TM helices in and out of the bicelle membrane.

claim: The four helices connected by peptide linkers can undergo the transition independently, although cooperative transitions of all four helices were observed.
source: The four helices connected by peptide linkers can undergo the transition independently, although we observed the cooperative transitions of all four helices.

claim: The transition of one part may energetically benefit adjacent parts for the same state by the geometrical perturbation of the accompanying insertion/extraction event.
source: The transition of one part may energetically benefit adjacent parts for the same state by the geometrical perturbation of the accompanying insertion/extraction event (as shown in Figure 6C).

claim: It is possible that, due to a limited spatiotemporal resolution, intermediate states during the transitions between the Uc and Uh states could not be detected.
source: It is also possible that, due to a limited spatiotemporal resolution, we could not detect possible intermediate states during the transitions between the Uc and Uh states.

claim: The folding pathway observed at 12 pN follows a strict progression from the Uc to Uh to I1,2 to N state, with no bypass of the middle Uh and I1,2 states.
source: The folding pathway observed at 12 pN follows a strict progression from the Uc to Uh to I1,2 to N state, with no bypass of the middle Uh and I1,2 states.

claim: The Uh state evidently serves as the primed state for the first helix-helix association of the Uh-to-I1,2 transition.
source: Thus, the Uh state evidently serves as the primed state for the first helix-helix association of the Uh-to-I1,2 transition (Figure 6C).

claim: The final I1,2-to-N transition involves two events: the second helix-helix association and the dimerization of two helical hairpins.
source: The final I1,2-to-N transition involves two events, i.e., the second helix-helix association and the dimerization of two helical hairpins.

claim: At 12 pN, two unassembled helices are separated by ~11 nm, whereas two helical hairpins that have not yet dimerized are very close with only ~1 nm by the intervening peptide linker.
source: At 12 pN, two unassembled helices are separated by ~11 nm, whereas two helical hairpins that have not yet dimerized are very close with only ~1 nm by the intervening peptide linker.

claim: Owing to the energetic penalty by the ~10 times greater distance, the helix-helix association is likely the rate-limiting step than the dimerization.
source: As a result, owing to the energetic penalty by the ~10 times greater distance, the helix-helix association is likely the rate-limiting step than the dimerization.

claim: The energy barriers for the Uh-to-I1,2 and I1,2-to-N transitions differ by only 0.5 kBT, which is less than the thermal energy level.
source: Indeed, the energy barriers for the Uh-to-I1,2 and I1,2-to-N transitions differ by only 0.5 kBT, which is less than the thermal energy level (Figure 6E).

claim: The formation of the other helical hairpin alone does not significantly contribute to the native fold stability.
source: This indicates that the formation of the other helical hairpin alone does not significantly contribute to the native fold stability.

claim: The steep free energy slope down the small bump observed between the I1,2 and N states may involve the final dimerization step.
source: This also reconciles the steep free energy slope down the small bump observed between the I1,2 and N states (Figure 6E), which may involve the final dimerization step.

claim: In the Kramers rate theory, τω is 2πγ/ωiωt in a high frictional regime such as protein folding.
source: Here, τω is 2πγ/ωiωt in a high frictional regime such as protein folding (Hagen, 2010), ωi and ωt are the angular frequencies that characterize the curvature of energy well and barrier top, and γ is the friction coefficient.

claim: The approach is a modification of a previous study where the frequency factor (kω=1/τω) was estimated for a soluble protein.
source: This approach is a modification of a previous study where the frequency factor (kω=1/τω) was estimated for a soluble protein (Gebhardt et al., 2010).

claim: It is necessary to acquire a large amount of extension data during the transitions using a high temporal resolution to estimate τω.
source: To this end, it is necessary to acquire a large amount of extension data during the transitions using a high temporal resolution.

claim: The temporal resolution of typical magnetic tweezers is inherently limited due to the camera-based method for the bead position tracking.
source: However, the temporal resolution of typical magnetic tweezers is inherently limited due to the camera-based method for the bead position tracking, which restricts the speed limit estimation.

claim: The robust single-molecule method overcomes the temporal resolution limitation by conducting prolonged observation of numerous transitions.
source: Our robust single-molecule method overcomes this limitation by conducting the prolonged observation of numerous transitions, resulting in the collection of abundant data points for each transition event.

claim: This experimental strategy would not be feasible with the previous magnetic tweezer method for membrane proteins, due to the less stable molecular tethering under applied forces.
source: This experimental strategy would not be feasible with the previous magnetic tweezer method for membrane proteins, due to the less stable molecular tethering under applied forces.

claim: In the limit of a high frictional regime, τω varies linearly with the friction coefficient γ, which reflects the external friction like solvent viscosity (ηs) and the internal friction (ηi).
source: In the limit of a high frictional regime, τω varies linearly with the friction coefficient γ, which reflects the external friction like solvent viscosity (ηs) and the internal friction (ηi) like dissipative intrachain interactions, concerted dihedral angle rotations, and non-native salt bridges (Hagen, 2010; Soranno et al., 2017; Chung et al., 2015; Qiu and Hagen, 2004).

claim: In extremely high viscous environments, the solvent viscosity becomes dominant for the friction term, leading to the relationship of τω ∝ γ ∝ ηs.
source: In extremely high viscous environments, the solvent viscosity become dominant for the friction term (Hagen, 2010; Eaton, 2021; Ansari et al., 1992), leading to the relationship of τω ∝ γ ∝ ηs.

claim: The approximate linear relationship between τω and ηs serves as a working hypothesis that can explain why the estimated τω time scale is in stark contrast to that of soluble proteins.
source: This approximate linear relationship between τω and ηs serves as a working hypothesis that can explain why our estimated τω time scale is in stark contrast to that of soluble proteins.

claim: The viscosity of lipid membranes was not measured in bicelles but rather in various other structures such as small to giant unilamellar vesicles and supported membranes, which could introduce possible errors into the analysis.
source: We note that the viscosity of lipid membranes was not measured in bicelles but rather in various other structures such as small to giant unilamellar vesicles and supported membranes, which could introduce possible errors into our analysis.

claim: Larger membrane proteins can fold via accrual of smaller structural units on the initial template.
source: A helical hairpin is the minimal structural size for helical membrane proteins that require the tertiary folding (Choi et al., 2019; Corin and Bowie, 2022; Krainer et al., 2018; Engelman and Steitz, 1981), although larger membrane proteins can fold via accrual of smaller structural units on the initial template (Choi et al., 2022; Corin and Bowie, 2022).

claim: The solvent friction is expected to be the primary determinant for τω in highly viscous lipid membrane environments.
source: In addition, the solvent friction is expected to be the primary determinant for τω in highly viscous lipid membrane environments (Ansari et al., 1992).

claim: The slowing effect of the coil-to-helix transition may be due to the transition itself that is a totally different process and/or the accompanying helix insertion into membranes.
source: The slowing effect may be due to the transition itself that is a totally different process and/or the accompanying helix insertion into membranes.

claim: The final folding step has a slightly slower time scale of ~50 ms for τω, which may be due to the additional dimerization step and/or the slight extraction of the unassembled helices of the I1,2 state from the membrane.
source: The final folding step, i.e., the helical hairpin formation followed by dimerization, has a slightly slower time scale of ~50 ms for τω. This slowing effect may be due to the additional dimerization step and/or the slight extraction of the unassembled helices of the I1,2 state from the membrane (as shown in Figure 6C).

claim: A covalent method using HaloTag and streptavidin can remain stable for 2 weeks.
source: Other covalent methods using HaloTag and streptavidin (Popa et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2015; Tapia-Rojo et al., 2023) can remain stable for 2 weeks.

claim: The time span of 2 weeks stability was the total duration for an unfolding-pulse experiment where the protein was subjected to a force jump to 45 pN for 45 s once a day, while being held at 4.3 pN throughout the days.
source: However, the time span was the total duration for an unfolding-pulse experiment where the protein was subjected to a force jump to 45 pN for 45 s once a day, while being held at 4.3 pN throughout the days (Popa et al., 2016).

claim: The same HaloTag tethering approach observed protein (un)folding transitions for ~8 hr at 4.5 pN and ~14 hr at 8.5 pN.
source: The same tethering approach observed protein (un)folding transitions for ~8 hr at 4.5 pN (Chen et al., 2015) and ~14 hr at 8.5 pN (Tapia-Rojo et al., 2023).

claim: All three widely used force-dependent kinetic models assume that the applied force is independent of the pre-exponential factor.
source: All three widely used force-dependent kinetic models assume that the applied force is independent of the pre-exponential factor as in τ(F) = τω∙exp(–ΔG†[F]/kBT) = τω∙f(ΔG†0,F,Δx), where ΔG†0 is the energy barrier height at zero force, F is the applied force, and Δx is the distance to the transition state (Hane et al., 2014).

claim: The deeper insertion of helices into the membrane at lower forces is effectively the rotation of already-inserted tilted helices toward the upright position.
source: Additionally, the deeper insertion of helices into the membrane at lower forces is effectively the rotation of already-inserted tilted helices toward the upright position.

claim: The helix rotation event also occurs at zero force, as the unassembled helices are tilted in a zigzag manner by the geometrical constraints at the intervening linkers.
source: The helix rotation event also occurs at zero force, as the unassembled helices are tilted in a zigzag manner by the geometrical constraints at the intervening linkers.

claim: The force-induced rotation of helices within the membrane does not involve different kinds of transitions, which likely manifest as an elevation of energy barrier heights.
source: Thus, the force-induced rotation of helices within the membrane does not involve different kinds of transitions, which likely manifest as an elevation of energy barrier heights.

claim: The argument about force-independence starts to break down as the soluble part on the membrane side opposite to the protein pulling side becomes dominant, which involves the transfer event between the membrane and water.
source: However, this argument starts to break down as the soluble part on the membrane side opposite to the protein pulling side becomes dominant, which involves the transfer event between the membrane and water.

source: In our case, the soluble portion is ~23% of the TM helical part in term of the number of amino acid residues.

claim: The estimated τω values for each transition would be valid at zero force within the error due to the transfer event.
source: Therefore, the estimated τω values for each transition would be valid at zero force within the error due to the transfer event.

source: Recently, Choi et al. measured the rate constants for helical hairpin formations in GlpG within bicelle membranes at low forces of 5–7 pN (Choi et al., 2019).

source: By extrapolating to zero force using Dudko-Hummer-Szabo model, the authors estimated the k0's corresponding to approximately 110–140 ms.

source: These values indeed do not exceed the ~20 ms speed limit for a helical hairpin formation we estimated here.

source: A high-speed atomic force microscopy with ~1 μs temporal resolution observed μs-rapid (un)folding transitions between numerous intermediates for bacteriorhodopsin (Yu et al., 2017).

source: However, the rapid transitions involve the coupled insertion and folding of a few amino acid residues from the fully unstructured polypeptide that is entirely exposed to an aqueous solution.

source: Therefore, the μs time scales for the conformational changes are not relevant to the speed limit of membrane protein folding within lipid bilayers.

source: This hypothesis reconciles the previous studies on the speed limit of soluble protein folding based on the Kramers theory.

source: In the limit of high solvent friction, the approximate linear viscosity dependency is also expected to hold for a more general Grote-Hynes theory, which incorporates time-dependent friction (Dupuis et al., 2018).

source: Simulation studies with soluble proteins have shown that changing solvent viscosity can alter folding pathways (Klimov and Thirumalai, 1997; Rhee and Pande, 2008), which may also be the case for membrane protein folding.

source: However, it would be challenging to observe experimentally as we must selectively control the membrane viscosity without impacting other properties.

source: Our estimates can be used to obtain more accurate parameters for membrane protein folding.
